Melsen ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0003-0062-1301 2 Show authors Nature Water ( 2026 ) Cite this article Save article View saved research 1792 Accesses 5 Altmetric Metrics details Abstract For five decades, refining models and datasets has been regarded as central to reducing uncertainty in global irrigation water withdrawal estimates. However, whether these efforts have succeeded remains unclear. Here we compile 1,624 global estimates from 65 studies published between 1974 and 2025 and evaluate them across 360 analytical pathways, spanning a comprehensive range of plausible statistical designs. Our results indicate that uncertainty in global irrigation water withdrawals has not declined: only 17% of pathways show any reduction over time, falling to 10% once projections to 2100 are excluded. The most common outcome is an increase in uncertainty (40% of pathways), followed by an unstable trend (34%). Progress may therefore require the field to renounce the goal of reducing uncertainty and instead double down on what it has historically done best: expanding it, until uncertainty reaches the boundary of what current knowledge of global irrigation cannot exclude. Environmental social sciences Hydrology Water resources Main The quantification of the volume of water globally withdrawn by irrigated agriculture has been a key hydrological goal since the Second World War 1 . Initially derived from statistical exercises and mostly produced through global hydrological models after 2000, global irrigation water withdrawal (IWW) estimates shape our understanding of irrigation’s impact on food, water and environmental security. Key assumptions—that irrigation accounts for 70% of freshwater withdrawals and 40% of food production 2 , exceeds the blue water planetary boundary 3 , 4 and depletes groundwater beyond sustainable limits 5 —are all grounded in IWW data. IWW figures also have strong policy implications: the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) use them under Sustainable Development Goal 6.4 (‘increase water-use efficiency across all sectors and ensure sustainable withdrawals’) 6 , whereas the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) integrate them into projections of land-use change and socio-climatic scenarios 7 , 8 , shaping narratives about future water availability. IWW estimates were deemed highly uncertain since the beginning. L’vovich 1 and Shiklomanov 9 identified the lack of empirical data due to uneven regional coverage as a major obstacle to accurate water accounting. Gleick 10 noted that these gaps were often filled with computed data, introducing pitfalls such as hidden assumptions, inadequate attention to uncertainties, variability in hydrological data and illusory precision. The FAO affirmed that modelled values, although valuable, ‘cannot replace local measurements ’ 11 . The issues of IWW numbers at the beginning of the 2000s were so obvious that caution was advised when using them because, jointly with industrial and domestic withdrawals, they were ‘the least reliable and most inconsistent of all water-resources information’ 12 . Reducing uncertainties to narrow down the spread of IWW estimates and bring them closer to the ‘true’ value was therefore seen as essential to advancing the field. This vision aligned with the notion of uncertainty as the antithesis of knowledge—something that research must seek to progressively eliminate 13 . Calls were issued to reduce uncertainties by producing more detailed maps of irrigated areas and crop types 14 , 15 , 16 , improving historical weather reconstruction and reanalysis products 17 , intensifying scientific collaborations 9 and adopting high-resolution modelling, remote sensing or machine learning 18 , 19 , 20 (Supplementary Text 1 ). The hydrological community responded accordingly: country-level and basin-scale estimates based on census statistics and fixed irrigation coefficients were replaced by spatially explicit, gridded models with remotely sensed irrigated areas, cropping calendars, historical climate forcing and coupled land-surface or hydrological models (Fig. 1 ). To date, the consideration of uncertainties as a transient stage to be overcome through finer-grained detail and more data remains the prevailing view in hydrological modelling 21 , 22 , 23 .
